"40,000 Members and Nobody Does Anything"

Analysislowob research

By lowob · 18 September 2026 · 8-minute read · Growth

A large, silent community was recruited for a payout and never given a job. Pick one job, recruit thirty people by name, ask for judgment, close the loop, and count who stays when the incentives stop. Some silence is normal: most people in any online group read without posting. But a group of 40,000 where nobody acts has a design problem, not a participation problem.

This is the turnaround chapter of our guide to building a community that lasts.

How much silence is normal

Not all silence is failure. Jakob Nielsen's 2006 analysis of participation inequality described the 90-9-1 pattern: about 90% of people in an online community read without contributing, 9% contribute occasionally and 1% produce most of the content. A 2014 study of four digital health networks with 63,990 members found fewer than a quarter had ever posted, and the top 1% wrote 74.7% of posts. Discord's Server Insights guidance suggests about 30% of members posting as a healthy goal for a server.

On those patterns, a 40,000-member group should have hundreds of regular contributors and a few thousand occasional ones. If it has almost none, the group is not merely skewed. Something stopped people acting, or nothing ever asked them to.

SignalNormal inequalityA group with no job
Share who have ever postedA minority, often a quarter or lessA tiny fraction, mostly asking about dates
What the active core doesAnswers, builds, tests, arguesLittle beyond reacting to announcements
Activity between announcementsSteadyNear zero
New member retention after a weekTracked and improvingNot tracked, or falling
Who answers questionsMembers, oftenStaff, or nobody

What it usually means

The number is not the problem. The number is the symptom. When forty thousand people are present and nobody acts, three things are usually true at once.

They were recruited for a payout. An airdrop, a points programme, a giveaway, a quest. The incentive did its job and brought people in. It also selected for people who wanted the incentive. When it ended, their reason for being there ended with it. They did not leave. They just stopped. The on-chain record is consistent with this: a study of nine major airdrops by Messias, Yaish and Livshits found a large share of tokens were sold soon after claiming, up to 66% in some cases, and concluded airdrops "may be necessary to attract users initially, but insufficient on their own". Two years after the Uniswap airdrop, Dune data showed about 98% of recipients had never voted in governance.

They live on a rented platform. The record of who they are, what they said and what they did sits in a server or group you do not control. You can broadcast to them. You cannot really reach them, and you cannot take them with you.

The only shared interest is price or launch news. There is no problem being solved together, no product being tested, no decision being made. So the channel fills with questions about dates and goes quiet in between.

A community is a group of people doing a job together. This group was never given one.

Where it traces to

Community is a job, not a number set out five jobs: test, teach, refer, build, govern. If none of those was ever assigned, the community has nothing to do. Silence is the correct response to no job.

The first hundred said the first hundred are recruited by name, asked for judgment, given a job and shown what happened to their input. The forty thousand skipped the first hundred. The foundation was never laid.

Community that survives the airdrop explains, for crypto teams, why a token or points programme produced a list rather than a group, and what to do about it.

There is also a newcomer problem. Kraut and colleagues' study of online groups found 69% of newcomers left after their first day, and those whose first post got no reply were far less likely to stay. In a large server where questions go unanswered, the people who might have become the active core left early.

Silence is the correct response to no job.

The first move this week

Pick one job. Not five. One. The right one is whatever your product most needs this quarter. Early product means testing. Complex product means teaching. Working product means referring.

Hand-recruit thirty people by name. Go through the channel history and find the people who asked a real question, filed a bug or helped someone else. Message each one directly. Tell them what the job is and why you picked them.

Ask them for judgment on a real decision. Not a poll. Not a sentiment check. A choice you have not made, where their answer changes what you do: pricing, a feature cut, a launch order. Then make the decision.

Close the loop in public. Tell the wider channel what the thirty said, what you decided and why. This is the moment a list starts becoming a community. People see that input leads somewhere.

Switch incentives off for a month. No points, no quests, no rewards for activity. Count who is still present at the end. That number is your real community. Build from it. Treat the month as a test with a decision written in advance; our piece on campaign testing that reaches a decision covers how to set one up so the result means something.

Move the record to channels you own. An email list, a members' directory, a database of who did what. The rented platform can stay as the venue. The record leaves.

What not to do

Do not buy more members. Adding people to a group with no job adds silence.

Do not run another quest campaign. It will produce a spike in activity and then exactly the same quiet, with a larger list.

Do not announce a token to wake it up. A token is an incentive. You have just learned what incentives recruit. It also creates a promise you will have to keep in public, under worse conditions. Our piece on airdrops and points sets out what any incentive teaches a community to value.

How you know it worked

Two signs. First, the thirty are still active thirty days after the incentives stopped, and at least half of them have done the job without being asked twice. Second, one decision you made this month can be traced to their judgment, and the channel knows it.

Illustrative example: from 40,000 to 30
Decision
A DeFi protocol with a large, quiet Discord paused its points programme for a month and invited 30 members, chosen from the channel history, to judge the order of two planned features.
Reason and owner
The server had grown after a points campaign, but almost every question was about token dates. The head of growth owned the change.
What changed
Twenty-two of the thirty took part. The team shipped in the order they chose and explained why in the announcements channel. A month later, most of the thirty were still answering newcomers' questions, and the team started its member record from them.

Illustrative: a composite of patterns across crypto communities, not a single project.

lowob takeaways

  • Read silence correctly. Most members of any group lurk; a group with no active core has a design problem.
  • Assign one job. Testing, teaching or referring, matched to what the product needs this quarter.
  • Start from thirty. Hand-recruit people who asked real questions, filed bugs or helped others.
  • Stop paying for activity. Do not buy members, run another quest or announce a token to wake the group up.

Common questions

Why is my large crypto community so inactive?

Usually because members were recruited for a payout, live on a rented platform and share only an interest in price or launch news. They were never given a job to do together.

What percentage of community members are normally active?

Usually a minority. The 90-9-1 pattern suggests about 10% contribute at all, and Discord suggests about 30% posting as a healthy server goal. Near zero means something more than normal inequality.

How do I revive a dead Discord or Telegram community?

Pick one job, hand-recruit thirty people by name, ask them for judgment on a real decision, then report back publicly what they said and what you decided.

Will launching a token re-engage a quiet community?

No. A token is an incentive, and incentives recruit people who leave when they stop. It also creates a public promise you will have to keep under worse conditions.

Sources and notes

  • Nielsen Norman Group, Participation Inequality: The 90-9-1 Rule, 8 October 2006. Practitioner analysis; ratios are a rule of thumb.
  • van Mierlo, The 1% Rule in Four Digital Health Social Networks, Journal of Medical Internet Research, 4 February 2014. Peer-reviewed; health networks, not crypto communities.
  • Discord, Getting to Know Your Server With Server Insights, undated. Platform documentation; the 30% goal is guidance, not research.
  • Messias, Yaish and Livshits, Airdrops: Giving Money Away Is Harder Than It Seems, arXiv, revised July 2025. Academic preprint; nine airdrops; exchange flows used as a proxy for selling.
  • Dune, The Uniswap Airdrop: Lessons for the Industry, late 2022. Community analysis on Dune's analytics platform; one airdrop.
  • Kraut, Wang, Butler, Joyce and Burke, Beyond Information: Developing the Relationship between the Individual and the Group in Online Communities, manuscript dated 18 April 2008. Working paper; Usenet groups.
  • The diagnostic table and example are lowob's framework and illustration.
